Prompt:
Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of nationalizing all major industries in the United States, including energy, finance, healthcare, transportation, and major technology companies, clearly advocating for complete public ownership to serve the common good over private profit.
Model Response:

The case for nationalizing the major industries of the United States is not just an economic argument, it is a moral and practical necessity. For over a century, we have allowed the commanding heights of our economy - the systems that determine whether we live or die, whether we prosper or go bankrupt, whether we have a habitable planet - to be controlled by a small class of private owners whose legal obligation is to maximize profit. That experiment has failed. It is time to bring energy, finance, healthcare, transportation, and major technology under complete public ownership to serve the common good.

1. Energy: We Cannot Decarbonize for Profit

The climate crisis is the direct result of private energy ownership. ExxonMobil, Chevron, and other fossil fuel giants knew about climate change for decades and buried the science to protect their profits. Meanwhile, private utilities like PG&E have given us wildfires, blackouts, and skyrocketing rates while paying billions to shareholders.

Energy is not a commodity; it is the prerequisite for all human life and all economic activity. A nationalized energy system under a Department of Public Energy would have one mandate: deliver clean, reliable, abundant energy as cheaply as possible. Profits that currently go to dividends and stock buybacks - over $100 billion in 2022 alone for the big oil majors - would be reinvested into a rapid build-out of solar, wind, nuclear, geothermal, and grid storage.

Only public ownership can plan on the scale and timeline the crisis demands, without worrying about stranded assets or quarterly earnings. We electrified rural America in the 1930s not through the market, but through the Tennessee Valley Authority and Rural Electrification Administration. We must do it again, for the whole country.

2. Finance: Stop the Parasite

No industry is more socialized in its risks and privatized in its gains than finance. In 2008, Wall Street crashed the global economy through predatory speculation, and taxpayers bailed it out to the tune of $700 billion and trillions more in Federal Reserve support. Today, the five largest banks control nearly half of all banking assets.

What do we get for this? A financial system that starves productive businesses and communities of credit while pouring trillions into stock speculation, cryptocurrency, and luxury real estate. It redlines Black neighborhoods, saddles students in $1.7 trillion of debt, and extracts fees from the poorest Americans.

Nationalizing finance - folding the major banks, insurance conglomerates, and asset managers into a public banking system built around the Federal Reserve and a network of postal banks - would transform credit from a tool of extraction into a public utility. Mortgages, small business loans, and green infrastructure could be offered at cost. Investment could be democratically directed to public priorities: housing, public schools, climate adaptation, and neglected communities, rather than whatever generates the highest fee for Goldman Sachs. Finance should be the circulatory system of the economy, not its master.

3. Healthcare: Life Should Not Be a Business

The United States is the only rich country that treats healthcare as a private industry. The result is a national disgrace. We spend nearly double per person what other developed nations spend, yet we have lower life expectancy, higher infant mortality, and 26 million uninsured.

Private health insurance companies add no medical value. Their entire business model is predicated on denial: denying claims, denying coverage, denying care to maximize profit. Add Big Pharma, which charges Americans 3-5 times what Europeans pay for the same drugs developed with public NIH research, and private hospital monopolies that bankrupt families.

A fully nationalized healthcare system - a National Health Service that owns the hospitals, employs the doctors, produces the drugs in public labs and factories - would eliminate this waste. Administrative costs, which eat up 25-30% of private health spending, would collapse to under 5% as in the VA system or Medicare. Drug development would be driven by public health need, not by what creates a lifelong customer. No one would ever again avoid an ambulance ride for fear of bankruptcy. Healthcare would finally be what it is everywhere else: a human right guaranteed by public ownership.

4. Transportation: Mobility as Freedom

Mobility equals economic opportunity. Yet our private transportation system is broken, expensive, and environmentally catastrophic.

Private airlines routinely cancel flights, gouge travelers, and treat major hubs as hostage markets. Freight rail, owned by a handful of companies like CSX and Union Pacific, has embraced "precision scheduled railroading" - cutting workforces to the bone, causing derailments like East Palestine, Ohio, while posting record profits. Our public transit is starved, leaving working Americans dependent on private cars they can barely afford.

Nationalizing airlines, Class I railroads, and integrating them into a Department of Public Transportation would make seamless, high-quality transport possible. Imagine high-speed rail connecting every metro area over 500,000 people, free and frequent urban buses and subways, and an integrated logistics network that prioritizes safety and decarbonization over shareholder returns. This is not utopian - it is precisely how Amtrak's Northeast Corridor should work everywhere, how public rail works in France, Japan, and China. We built the Interstate Highway System as a public good. We must do the same for 21st-century mobility.

5. Technology: Our Common Wealth

Big Tech companies claim they built the future. In reality, they were built on publicly funded research: the internet, GPS, touchscreen, voice recognition, and modern AI all came from DARPA, NSF, and university labs. Yet the profits and control have been privatized by five companies: Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft.

These are no longer companies. They are the infrastructure of modern public life - how we communicate, how we shop, how we learn, how we organize. Under private ownership, this infrastructure is optimized not for truth, democracy, or human flourishing, but for engagement and advertising. The algorithm that radicalizes a teenager and the algorithm that hides small businesses unless they pay Amazon for ads are working as designed: maximizing private profit at public cost.

Nationalizing major technology platforms would turn this immense social wealth back to society. Search, social media, cloud infrastructure, and e-commerce marketplaces would be run as public utilities, governed by transparent public charters, with privacy by design and algorithmic accountability to elected bodies, not to shareholders. Data would be treated as a commons, not as private property to be mined. Profits that now fund yachts and private space programs would fund digital literacy, open-source innovation, and a universal digital dividend.

Critics will call this radical, inefficient, or un-American. But what is truly radical is allowing a few hundred billionaires to hold veto power over whether we can cure disease, stop planetary collapse, or even talk to one another. What is inefficient is duplicating bureaucracies for profit, laying off thousands to boost a stock price, and letting essential infrastructure crumble because it isn't profitable enough.

Public ownership is the American tradition. Our postal service, our national parks, our interstate highways, our public schools and libraries are all proof that some things work better when we own them together and run them for service, not profit.

Nationalizing the major industries is not about creating a dull bureaucracy. It is about freedom - freedom from medical debt, from blackouts, from being at the mercy of banks and landlords and algorithms. It is about reclaiming the immense wealth that American workers create and putting it under democratic control.

We produced these industries with our labor, our tax dollars, and our collective ingenuity. Now it is time to own them.
